exhibits.title: Painted Caves

when.display: at least 51,200 years ago (Sulawesi); c. 36,000 years ago (Chauvet)

site.label: Leang Karampuang and Leang Tedongnge, Sulawesi

regions.note: A continuous rock-art tradition of great antiquity.

exhibits.change: Animals, people and scenes appeared on stone — images that stand for things.
exhibits.context: Uranium-series dating in Sulawesi places a painted scene of humans and a pig at least 51,200 years ago, and a warty pig at least 45,500. In Europe, Chauvet Cave's lions, horses and rhinoceroses are about 36,000 years old. Rock art traditions arose on several continents.
exhibits.significance: Figurative images show minds able to represent absent things — the same capacity later used for writing, maps and diagrams.

uncertainty.note: Minimum ages: the art may be older than the crusts dated over it. Early art probably arose independently in several regions.

sources.note: Oktaviana et al. 2024, Nature; Brumm et al. 2021, Science Advances; Quiles et al. 2016 (Chauvet).

exhibits.title: The Eyed Needle

regions.note: Common in Europe from c. 26,000 years ago.

exhibits.change: Thread through an eye: fitted, layered clothing for the cold.
exhibits.context: Bone needles with drilled eyes appear in southern Siberia and the Caucasus by about 45,000–40,000 years ago. Tailored clothing let people live through the harshest phases of the Ice Age.
exhibits.significance: Fitted clothing opened the far north — and eventually the route to the Americas.

exhibits.title: The First Instruments

site.label: Hohle Fels and Geissenklösterle, Swabian Jura

exhibits.change: Flutes of bird bone and mammoth ivory — music you could carry.
exhibits.context: Flutes made from griffon vulture and swan bone, and a more difficult one carved from ivory, come from the caves of the Swabian Jura, among the oldest musical instruments known.
exhibits.significance: Music as an organised, shared activity — possibly bonding larger social networks.

exhibits.title: The Lion-Man
exhibits.change: A figure that exists nowhere in nature: a human body with a lion's head.
exhibits.context: Carved from mammoth ivory and about 31 cm tall, the figurine was reconstructed from hundreds of fragments. Making it would have taken many hours with stone tools.
exhibits.significance: An imagined being — evidence of myth, story and minds combining ideas freely.

exhibits.title: The Hohle Fels Figurine
exhibits.change: The oldest known sculpture of a human body.
exhibits.context: A small ivory female figure with a ring in place of a head, found in 2008, perhaps worn as a pendant. Later Ice Age figurines are found from France to Siberia.
exhibits.significance: Part of a long, widespread tradition of portable art across Ice Age Eurasia.

exhibits.title: The Sungir Burials
exhibits.change: Thousands of ivory beads, once sewn onto clothing, lay with the dead.
exhibits.context: Graves of an adult and two children contained more than 10,000 ivory beads, spears straightened from mammoth tusk and carved ornaments. Each bead took long hours to make.
exhibits.significance: Enormous labour invested in the dead implies social roles and shared beliefs.

exhibits.title: Ohalo II
exhibits.change: A camp where wild wheat and barley were gathered, ground — and perhaps tended.
exhibits.context: Waterlogged remains at Ohalo II preserved brush huts, grass bedding, a grinding slab with starch, and seeds of wild cereals, with weeds that hint at small-scale trial cultivation, some 11,000 years before farming.
exhibits.significance: Shows how deep the roots of agriculture run — farming grew out of long familiarity with wild plants.

uncertainty.note: Whether anything was deliberately cultivated here is debated.

exhibits.title: Fishhooks
exhibits.change: Curved shell hooks let people catch fish they could not reach with spears.
exhibits.context: Shell fishhooks from Sakitari Cave in Okinawa are about 23,000 years old; Jerimalai on Timor has hooks from roughly the same period. Island peoples of the western Pacific were skilled marine foragers.
exhibits.significance: Marine resources sustained island life — skills later central to the settlement of the Pacific.

sources.note: Fujita et al. 2016, PNAS; O'Connor et al. 2011, Science.

exhibits.title: Into the Americas

when.display: by c. 16,000 years ago; White Sands footprints suggest 23,000–21,000 years ago

regions.note: Beringia, the land bridge between Asia and America.

exhibits.change: People reached the last habitable continents — the Americas.
exhibits.context: Ancestors of Indigenous Americans came from northeast Asia via Beringia. Monte Verde in southern Chile was occupied about 14,500 years ago; human footprints at White Sands have been dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum.
exhibits.significance: Humans now lived on every continent except Antarctica — and the Americas would go on to invent agriculture, cities and writing independently.

uncertainty.note: The timing and route (coastal or interior) of the first arrivals are actively debated; the White Sands dates are contested but have been supported by further tests.

sources.note: Bennett et al. 2021; Pigati et al. 2023, Science; Dillehay 1997 (Monte Verde).

exhibits.title: Pottery

when.display: c. 20,000 years ago in East Asia; independently later in Africa and the Americas

site.label: Odai Yamamoto I, Aomori (c. 16,000 years ago)

exhibits.change: Clay transformed by fire into waterproof containers — cooking and storing changed.
exhibits.context: Pottery fragments from Xianrendong Cave in China are about 20,000 years old, made by hunter-gatherers, not farmers. Pottery was invented again, independently, in the Sahara around 9400 BCE and in South America. In the Near East it came after farming.
exhibits.significance: Boiling, fermenting and storing food changed diets and made new foods edible. Kilns later led to glazes, glass and metal smelting.

uncertainty.note: Pottery arose independently several times; its link to farming differs by region.

sources.note: Wu et al. 2012, Science (Xianrendong); Huysecom et al. 2009 (Ounjougou).

exhibits.title: The Ishango Bone
exhibits.change: Groups of notches on a bone handle — a tally, or something more?
exhibits.context: The Ishango bone carries columns of notches in groups; some researchers see counting or even a lunar calendar, others simple tallying or decoration. Older notched bones, such as Lebombo in southern Africa, may also be tallies.
exhibits.significance: External marks that store quantities are a first step toward numbers and writing.

uncertainty.note: Mathematical interpretations beyond simple tallying are speculative.

exhibits.title: The Spear-Thrower
exhibits.change: A hooked lever lengthened the arm and hurled darts much faster.
exhibits.context: The oldest surviving spear-thrower hook is of antler, from the Solutrean in France. The device was used across the world, including the Australian woomera and the Mesoamerican atlatl.
exhibits.significance: A simple lever that multiplied human force — mechanics in the hand.

uncertainty.note: Wooden spear-throwers rarely survive; the device is probably older.

exhibits.title: Lascaux
exhibits.change: Hundreds of animals painted and engraved deep underground.
exhibits.context: Discovered in 1940, Lascaux holds some 600 painted animals and nearly 1,500 engravings, made with mineral pigments by lamplight and scaffolding.
exhibits.significance: A late masterpiece of a tradition that by then was tens of thousands of years old.

exhibits.title: The First Domestic Animal

when.display: undisputed dogs by c. 15,000 years ago; genetic estimates reach further back

regions.note: Some genetic studies point to Siberia.

exhibits.change: Wolves became dogs — the first partnership between people and another species.
exhibits.context: The earliest undisputed dog, buried with two humans at Bonn-Oberkassel about 14,200 years ago, had been cared for through illness. Dogs were domesticated by hunter-gatherers, thousands of years before farming.
exhibits.significance: A model for later domestication, and a working companion in hunting, herding and hauling.

uncertainty.note: Where, when and how many times dogs were domesticated remain unresolved.

exhibits.title: Houses of Mammoth Bone
exhibits.change: Treeless plains were settled with dwellings framed by mammoth bones.
exhibits.context: At Mezhyrich and similar sites on the East European plain, circular structures were built from hundreds of mammoth bones, probably covered with hides.
exhibits.significance: Architecture shaped by local materials in one of the harshest environments humans lived in.
